title: Kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ: five verses against obstructing forces
theme: A reference, by their opening words, to five verses to Agni that the reciter supplies from the Saṃhitā; the commentators take them as prayers to remove what obstructs.

words.role: first word of the verse cited
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «पाजो बलमस्मभ्यं कृणुष्व कुरुष्व» — make strength for us

words.meaning: thus — marks the words before it as a quotation

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «इत्याद्या ऋचः पञ्च» — the five verses beginning so

sandhi.type: -aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: Before a vowel other than a, -aḥ loses its visarga (it becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)), leaving the vowels apart: pājaḥ + iti → pāja iti.

morphology.note: This anuvāka is a pratīka: it gives only the opening words of a passage, kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ, and the number of verses, pañca, and the reciter supplies the rest from the Saṃhitā. The commentators identify the five verses (see below).

translation.readable: Here are recited the five verses that begin ‘Spread out your strength …’.

syntax: Not a sentence but a citation: the opening words of a verse, the particle iti marking them as quoted, and the number of verses meant.

ambiguities.note: Addressed to Agni to strike at demons with his flames. The anonymous commentator reads the enemies as also inner ones — desire, anger and the like («कामक्रोधादिशत्रुसंहारार्थं»); Bhāskara says that here, by the context, they are to be explained as setting out Brahman.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: The anuvāka itself is a citation of 9 syllables. The verses it cites are metrical: the anonymous commentator calls them anuṣṭubh («पञ्चानुष्टुप्छन्दस्का»), though the first line he quotes, kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīṃ yāhi rājevāmavāṁ ibhena, has two eleven-syllable pādas.

beginner: This anuvāka has only four words: ‘Spread out your strength … thus, five.’ It is a pointer, not a text. Reciters knew a large body of verses by heart, so a book could name a passage by its first words and the number of verses, and the reciter would supply the rest. The commentators say where the five verses are found: in the first book of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, at the end of its second chapter. They are verses to Agni, the god of fire, asking him to drive away hostile forces with his flames. One commentator explains that in this part of the Upaniṣad, which concerns release, the hostile forces are also inner ones, such as desire and anger. The anuvāka points to the verses; it says nothing about what reciting them brings.
analogy: Like a hymn book that prints only ‘Hymn 27, verses 1–5’: the singers know the words; the page only says which.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names the five verses beginning kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ, to be recited in full.

commentary.q: Where are the five verses, and how are they used?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa place them in the first book of the Saṃhitā, at the close of its second chapter: «संहितायाः प्रथमकाण्डे द्वितीयप्रपाठकस्यान्तिमानुवाके समाम्नाताः» (Sāyaṇa), and say they are to be recited quietly, «ऋचः पञ्च जपितव्या इति शेषः». The anonymous commentator gives all five with an explanation, and names the seer as Vāmadeva and the deity as Agni: «वामदेवदृष्टा अग्निदेवताकाः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Having pointed to rites as aids to purity of mind in this section on release, the text now gives mantras that remove obstacles, says the anonymous commentator: «चित्तशुद्धिहेतूनां कर्मणां संग्रहेणोपयोगमस्मिन्मोक्षप्रकरणे सूचयित्वा». The fruit of praying to Agni, he says, is that enemies outside and within cease: «अस्मिन्मन्त्रे बाह्माभ्यन्तरशत्रुनिवृत्तिरग्निप्रार्थनायाः फलम्». Bhāskara: the five are demon-slaying verses used in the worship of the god in the form of fire, «इत्यादयः पञ्च राक्षोघ्न्यो ऽग्नयात्मनो देवस्य उपासनादौ विनियोज्याः», and here they are to be explained as setting out Brahman, «ताश्चात्र प्रकरणानुरोधाद् ब्रह्मप्रतिपादकतया व्याख्येयाः».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The commentators agree on what the five verses are; they differ on how to read them here — against inner enemies (the anonymous commentator), or as teaching Brahman (Bhāskara).

contemporary.text: A pratīka trusts the reader to carry the rest of the passage in memory. It is a reminder that many texts were made to be completed by people who already knew them, and that reading such a text well can mean knowing what it leaves out. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Can you think of a song or saying you would recognise from its first few words? What lets a few words stand for the whole?
reflect.deeper: The commentators read verses about demons as also about inner enemies. When is it fair to read a text’s outer images as inner ones?
reflect.practice: Name one inner ‘obstacle’ — a habit of mind — that got in your way today, without judging it.

references.text: The Tirupati e-text writes out the five verses in full after the pratīka; the base and the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text give only the pratīka (corrections.json, variant).

Sāyaṇa comments on this anuvāka as his anuvāka 20 (the concordance maps it correctly). Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s comment is his anuvāka 20; the edition’s concordance gives no Bhāskara anuvāka for 10.27, so it is cited here by his own number.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text expands the pratīka into the five verses; this edition keeps the base, which cites them by their opening words, as the Ānandāśrama text also does.
The anonymous commentator calls the five verses anuṣṭubh, but the verse lines he quotes have eleven-syllable pādas; his metre statement could not be confirmed from the files.
Concordance: Bhāskara’s anuvāka 20 comments on this pratīka, but the edition’s map lists nothing for 10.27.
